articles.title: What Is SEER2? The Complete 2026 Homeowner Efficiency Guide
articles.excerpt: Learn what the new DOE SEER2 testing standards mean for your next HVAC purchase, energy savings calculations, and sizing.
articles.content:
The Department of Energy officially raised the baseline efficiency requirement for all residential air conditioning and heat pump systems to SEER2 (Seasonal Energy Efficiency Ratio 2).

### What Does SEER2 Measure?
SEER2 measures the total cooling output in BTUs divided by the total electric energy input in watt-hours over a typical cooling season, using an updated M1 testing procedure that simulates real-world duct static pressure (0.5 in. w.g.) rather than artificial laboratory conditions.

### What Should You Buy?
- **Standard Baseline (14.3 to 15.2 SEER2)**: Affordable upfront cost, reliable single-stage or two-stage performance.
- **High-Performance Inverter (18 to 24 SEER2)**: Whisper-quiet, superior dehumidification, and maximum energy savings. Over a 15-year operational lifespan, an 18+ SEER2 system saves an average of $6,800 in cumulative electric costs compared to an older 10-SEER unit.

articles.title: Heat Pumps vs. Traditional AC & Gas Furnace: What Makes Sense for Your Home?

articles.content:
Homeowners face a major question when replacing aging HVAC equipment: Should you stick with a traditional split system (central AC paired with a gas furnace or electric air handler), or upgrade to a modern high-efficiency inverter heat pump?

### How Inverter Heat Pumps Changed the Game
Historically, older heat pumps struggled during extreme cold snaps, blowing lukewarm "cool-warm" air and triggering expensive electric resistance heat strips. Modern variable-speed inverter heat pumps (such as the Bosch IDS or Trane XV series) modulate seamlessly from 25% to 100% capacity. They maintain precise indoor temperatures, dehumidify 30% more effectively in muggy humid summers, and supply 100% heating capacity down to single digits.

### Cost Breakdown & Tax Incentives:
- **Inflation Reduction Act (25C)**: Heat pumps qualify for up to $2,000 in federal tax credits compared to only $600 for high-efficiency conventional ACs.
- **Local Utility Rebates**: Local electric and gas utility providers offer tiered rebates for variable-capacity heat pumps.
- **Operating Costs**: Because heat pumps operate in heating mode with a Coefficient of Performance (COP) between 3.0 and 4.0—meaning they deliver 3 to 4 units of heat energy for every 1 unit of electricity consumed.

articles.title: Why Is My AC Unit Freezing Up in the Summer? (And What to Do)
articles.excerpt: Discover why ice forms on your air conditioner coils even when it is 100°F outside, and the critical steps to protect your compressor from catastrophic failure.
articles.content:
Finding a solid block of ice encasing your copper refrigerant lines or indoor evaporator coil on a scorching summer afternoon is startling. How can ice form when summer heat is raging?

### The Thermodynamics of Coil Freeze-Up
Your air conditioner does not create cold; it removes heat from indoor air. Refrigerant expands inside the indoor evaporator coil at temperatures typically between 40°F and 45°F. However, if the balance between refrigerant pressure and indoor airflow is disrupted, the coil temperature drops below 32°F (freezing). Condensation immediately freezes on the aluminum fins. As ice builds, it acts as an insulator, blocking airflow further until the entire coil becomes a solid block of ice.

### The 3 Most Common Causes:
1. **Severe Airflow Restriction**: A dirty, dust-choked air filter prevents warm indoor air from passing over the coil. With no heat to absorb, the refrigerant remains below freezing.
2. **Refrigerant Leaks**: Low refrigerant charge causes a drastic drop in evaporator coil pressure, lowering the boiling point below 32°F.
3. **Failing Blower Motor or Collapsed Ductwork**: If the blower fan fails to push adequate CFM across the coil, freezing occurs within 15 to 30 minutes.

### Immediate Steps to Take:
- **Step 1**: Turn your thermostat from COOL to OFF immediately.
- **Step 2**: Switch the FAN setting from AUTO to ON. This forces ambient room air over the coil to thaw the ice without running the compressor.
- **Step 3**: Check your air filter. If gray with dust, replace it immediately.
- **Step 4**: Call a certified technician. Do NOT attempt to chip ice away with sharp tools, as aluminum evaporator tubing punctures easily!

sections.name: Emergency Dispatch Header
sections.heading: 24/7 Emergency AC & Heating Dispatch
sections.subheading: Extreme heat and winter freezes pose real hazards. Our on-call master technicians are stationed across our primary service territory with target on-site arrival under 2 hours.

sections.name: Qualifying Conditions
sections.heading: Qualifying Emergency Conditions
sections.subheading: Situations that receive priority queue placement and expedited on-site technician dispatch.

items.title: Complete Cooling Failure
items.description: Outdoor temperatures exceed 90°F with infants, senior citizens, or health-vulnerable residents in the home.

items.title: Complete Heating Loss in Freezing Weather
items.description: Outdoor temperatures fall below 40°F, risking interior freeze damage and burst plumbing pipes.

items.title: Active Water Leaks from Ceiling or Attic
items.description: Condensate pan overflow threatening ceiling drywall, insulation, and home structural integrity.

items.title: Electrical Burning Smells or Sparking
items.description: Immediate fire safety triage: switch system OFF at main circuit breaker and contact dispatch immediately.

sections.name: What to Do While Waiting
sections.heading: What to Do While Technician is En Route
sections.subheading: Protect your family and HVAC equipment before the service van arrives.

items.title: 1. Shut Off Power at Thermostat
items.description: Set system switch to OFF. Running a seized compressor or frozen coil causes irreversible motor burnout.

items.title: 2. Check Your Main Air Filter
items.description: A completely blocked filter starves the system of air and freezes the evaporator coil within hours.

items.title: 3. Clear Access Path to Attic & Outdoor Unit
items.description: Ensure our technician can safely access the breaker panel, attic stairs, and outdoor condenser.

items.title: How much does a routine AC diagnostic cost?
items.description: Our standard diagnostic fee is $89. During this visit, a NATE-certified master technician performs a 21-point electrical, airflow, and mechanical evaluation. Crucially: when you approve any recommended repair, 100% of the $89 fee is credited toward the repair cost.

items.title: Do you charge extra for evening or weekend emergency calls?
items.description: For Comfort Club members, there are zero overtime surcharges 365 days a year. For non-members, we charge a flat upfront $149 emergency dispatch fee disclosed before our rolling warehouse departs—with no hidden hourly surprises.

items.title: Why is water dripping from my ceiling or indoor AC closet?
items.description: This indicates a clogged primary condensate drain line (usually algae/bacteria sludge build-up) or a cracked drain pan. If water is backing up, turn off the AC immediately to prevent drywall damage and electrical short-circuits. Our technicians use high-pressure nitrogen to clear the line and treat the pan with long-lasting biocides.

items.title: How often should I change my HVAC air filter?
items.description: Standard 1-inch pleated filters should be inspected monthly and replaced every 30 to 60 days, especially during hot summer months and heavy pollen seasons. High-efficiency 4-inch to 5-inch media filters only need replacement every 6 to 12 months.

items.title: What is the lifespan of a modern air conditioning and heating system?
items.description: Due to peak cooling seasons and steady summer runtime, the average lifespan of a central AC is 10 to 14 years. Well-maintained systems enrolled in annual preventive maintenance regularly reach 15 to 18 years.

items.title: Can I qualify for clean energy tax credits and utility rebates?
items.description: Yes. Under federal energy efficiency guidelines, qualifying high-efficiency heat pumps (16+ SEER2) can earn up to a $2,000 tax credit. Additionally, local utility providers frequently provide tiered instant equipment rebates.
